It is a pseudo-addiction and so the "why do you do it" can be hard to articulate.

Its allure is similar to Facebook in the sense that you don't go there looking for anything specific, rather, you go to be entertained. It's not dissimilar from the way you turn on the TV without knowing what you're going to end up watching, you just look around, and see what's on. Except instead of a few hundred channels to choose from, it's the entire internet.

I'd say there are 2 things that keep me coming back to Reddit:

(1) The fact that more entertaining, topical, "better" content floats to the top. Millions of people scan the furthest reaches of the internet and post things they find interesting, ridiculous, or noteworthy, and the community votes to banish things to oblivion or exalt them to the forefront. Depending on the day, the front page can make it look like a news site, a humor site, a gamer site, or music site.

When Bin Laden was killed, I heard it first on Reddit; when the Aurora shooting happened, the most up-to-date and detailed info was on Reddit (as described here: http://techcrunch.com/2012/07/20/reddit-aurora-shooting/ ); or when a new meme starts making the rounds, I'll probably see it first on Reddit. It is no more or less a serious news source than a purveyor of cat videos.

(2) The commentary can be as interesting as the content. The huge user base makes for a colorful comment section, and, as with the content, the most insightful comments generally rise to the top. Every 2 or 3 weeks, someone will post something from a scientific journal of questionable validity claiming to have found the miracle cure for "X" (you name it), and if it looks interesting it might get enough votes to find its way to the front page. Under the Reddit microscope, you can bet that the top of the comment section will have a multi-paragraph explanation written by an experienced neuroscientist/biologist/climatologist/etc. that details why the article is terribly written and under-researched, or alternatively, why it's genuinely cause for excitement.

On the flipside, the commentary can be an exercise in Groupthink of the highest order, a manic parade of trolls and circlejerks that would rather humiliate an OP for lulz than maintain any sort of civilized discourse. But, hey, it's the internet. What did you expect?

However, the groupthink can also be a lot of fun especially when combined with the gamification" side of reddit, I really enjoy karma. However, my feeling is the community has grown to what it has because of the quality of its content and diverse commenters. Karma chasers.and other novelties like copypasta are cool too.

There is also the whole community creation and building side to it . I really enjoy this as it is is like a less narcissist facebook/twitter challenge.
